analysis.one_liner: Extends federal debt-collection protections to small businesses with debts under $5 million.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 29–24 on June 22, 2022, but it never reached the House floor and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bans harassing calls, false threats, and other abusive tactics — but only for consumer debts, not business debts. This bill would have made those same rules apply when a debt collector goes after a small business, for any non-equity debt under $5 million. It would also have placed limits on what collectors can report to commercial credit bureaus. The bill cleared a committee vote but never got a vote in the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Small business owners — restaurants, contractors, family firms — who are personally hounded by collectors over a business debt. They would get the same protections consumers already have: limits on harassment, false statements, and unfair collection methods, plus restrictions on what collectors can pass along to commercial credit bureaus that decide a business's creditworthiness.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small business owners facing debt collectors

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to small business debt 'to the same extent as this Act applies to debt of consumers,' covering non-equity obligations under $5 million owed by partnerships, corporations, trusts, estates, cooperatives, associations, and other entities. [S3]

Redefines 'debt' under the Act as any obligation to pay money arising from a transaction, whether or not a court judgment has been entered, so collection abuses on unpaid business debts are covered. [S3]

Extends the Act's rules to collectors' dealings with commercial credit bureaus, which currently assemble and sell credit reports on businesses, mirroring the limits that apply to consumer reporting agencies. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection agencies and commercial credit bureaus, which would face new legal restrictions and compliance costs on business collections. Those costs could partly reach small businesses if collectors charge more for regulated collection work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Debt collection agencies and commercial credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act was written for individuals, and extending it to entities could bring friction: businesses large and small borrow through contracts and invoicing where aggressive-but-legal pressure is part of normal commercial practice, and stricter rules could slow routine collections. [S3]

The $5 million threshold covers sizable corporations, trusts, and even government agencies, not just mom-and-pop shops, so compliance costs for collection firms would be broad and could be passed back to business customers through higher collection fees. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and focused: owners of small firms would no longer face collection tactics the law already deems too abusive to use on individuals. The cost is a compliance burden on collection agencies and credit bureaus, some of which would likely flow back to businesses as fees. On balance the bill asks an industry to follow rules it already applies elsewhere, rather than asking the public to fund anything.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared a Financial Services Committee vote 29–24 in June 2022, but the House never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Lawson (D-FL) introduced the bill on February 22, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services. [S5]
On June 22, 2022, the committee considered and marked up the bill and ordered it reported as amended by a 29–24 vote. [S5]
No further action was ever taken: the bill was never reported to the full House under the record's history and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection agencies and commercial credit bureaus stay free of the consumer-style rules on business debts. Small business owners remain unprotected from the same tactics that are illegal when used on individuals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Collection agencies and commercial credit bureaus

for.name: Rep. Al Lawson, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: 29 House Financial Services Committee members
for.what_they_did: Voted yes in committee to order the bill reported as amended, 29–24.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee minority
against.what_they_did: Voted no in the June 22, 2022 markup, contributing to the narrow 29–24 margin.

against.name: House majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote; the bill received no action after committee and died at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote was close at 29–24, but the record does not include party breakdowns for the markup, and with zero cosponsors there is no broader measure of cross-party support.

industries.note: The bill would subject collections on small business debts to the same anti-harassment and anti-fraud rules that already apply to consumer debts, limiting tactics the industry can currently use in the commercial space. For small business owners, those rules are the same protection consumers already get.

The bill defines commercial credit bureaus and applies portions of the Act to their interactions with collectors, restricting what can be reported while a debt is disputed — a first-ever federal constraint on business credit reporting under this law. Small businesses' credit standing depends on these bureaus, so the protections run with the public's interest.
